title: De Carnis Resurrectione
author: Tertullian
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0275.stoa026.opp-lat2, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: at ego magis ridebo uulgus tunc, cum ipsos quoque defunctos atrocissime exurit, quos postmodum gulosissime nutrit, isdem ignibus et promerens et offendens. o pietatem de crudelitate ludentem! sacrificat an insultat, cum crematis cremat? plane cum uulgo interdum et sapientes sententiam suam iungunt. nihil esse post mortem Epicuri schola est. ait et Seneca omnia post mortem finiri, etiam ipsam. satis est autem, si non minor philosophia Pythagorae et Empedoclis et Platonici immortalem animam e contrario reclamant, immo adhuc proxime etiam in corpora remeabilem adfirmant.
passages.english: But I will laugh at the common crowd all the more when it most savagely burns up those very dead whom it afterwards feeds most gluttonously, both earning their favour and offending them with the same fires. What piety, making sport out of cruelty! Is it sacrificing or insulting, when it burns [offerings] to the burned? Indeed the wise too sometimes join their opinion to the crowd's. That there is nothing after death is the teaching of the school of Epicurus. Seneca too says that all things are ended after death, even [death] itself. It is enough, however, that the no lesser philosophy of Pythagoras and Empedocles, and the Platonists, cry out on the contrary that the soul is immortal, and indeed go further and affirm that it can even return into bodies.
passages.notes: 'Platonici' is read as the Platonists (perhaps 'of the Platonist', i.e. Plato). 'proxime' ("go further") is uncertain in sense.

passages.original: nulli denique alii salutem corporali substantiae inuident quam alterius diuinitatis haeretici. ideoque et Christum aliter disponere coacti, ne creatoris habeatur, in ipsa prius carne\' eius errauerunt, aut nullius ueritatis contendentes eam secundum Marcionem et Basiliden aut propriae qualitatis secun-I dum haereses Valentini et Appellen. atque ita sequitur, ut salutem eius substantiae excludant, cuius Christum consortem negant, certi illam summo praeiudicio resurrectionis instrue-I tam, si iam in Christo resurrexit caro.
passages.english: In short, none but the heretics of another divinity begrudge salvation to the bodily substance. And so, being compelled to arrange Christ too in a different way, so that he may not be held to be the Creator's, they first went astray concerning his very flesh, contending either that it had no reality, following Marcion and Basilides, or that it was of a peculiar quality, following the heresies of Valentinus and Apelles. And so it follows that they exclude from salvation that substance of which they deny that Christ was a sharer, being certain that it is furnished with the highest precedent for resurrection if the flesh has already risen in Christ.
passages.notes: Scanning artefacts removed: the stray mark after "carne" and the line-break hyphens in "secun-dum" and "instrue-tam". "Praeiudicio" is taken in its legal sense of a prior ruling or precedent. "Appellen" is read as Apelles, the disciple of Marcion.

passages.original: animae autem salutem credo retractatu carere. omnes enim fere haeretici eam, quoquo modo uolunt, tamen non negant. uiderit unus aliqui Lucanus nec huic quidem substantiae parcens, quam secundum Aristotelem dissoluens aliud quid pro ea subicit, tertium quiddam resurrecturus, neque anima neque caro, id est non homo, sed ursus forsitan, qua Lucanus. habet et iste a nobis plenissimum (de omni statu animae\' stilum.
passages.english: The salvation of the soul, however, I believe needs no discussion. For almost all the heretics, in whatever way they like, still do not deny it. Let one Lucan or other look to himself, who does not spare even this substance, but, dissolving it after Aristotle, substitutes something else in its place, so as to rise again as some third thing, neither soul nor flesh, that is, not a man, but perhaps a bear, as Lucan [is]. He too has from us a very full treatment on the whole condition of the soul.
passages.notes: 'qua Lucanus' is obscure, probably a pun on the name (Lucan/Lucanian, where 'Lucanian ox' was a name for the elephant, or bears of Lucania); the sense is uncertain. Lucan here is the Marcionite heretic. The stray parenthesis and quotation mark in the text are scanning artefacts; the treatise referred to is Tertullian's work on the soul.

passages.original: Igitur quoniam et rudes quique de communibus adhuc sensibus sapiunt et dubii et simplices per eosdem sensus denuo inquietantur et ubique in primis iste in nos aries temperatur, quo carnis condicio quassatur, necessario et a nobis carnis primum condicio munietur, uitupera.tione laudatione depulsa. ita nos rhetoricari quoque prouocant haeretici, sicut etiam philosophari. futtile et frioulu istud corpusculum, quod malum denique appellare non horrent, etsi angelorum fuisset operatio, ut Menandro et Marco placet, etsi ignei alicuius extructio aeque angeli, ut Appelles docet, sufficeret ad auctoritatem carnis secundae diuinitatis patrocinium. angelos post deum nouimus. iam nunc quisquis ille summus deus haeretici cuiusque est, non inmerito ab ipso quoque deducerem carnis dignitatem, a quo uoluntas producendae ei adfuisset utique enim prohibuisset fieri quam fieri scisset, si fieri noluisset.
passages.english: Therefore, since all the uninstructed still think according to common notions, and the doubtful and simple are unsettled afresh by those same notions, and everywhere this battering ram is above all directed against us, by which the condition of the flesh is shaken, we too must of necessity first fortify the condition of the flesh, repelling disparagement by praise. So the heretics provoke us to play the rhetorician as well as the philosopher. This futile and frivolous little body, which in the end they do not shrink from calling evil, even if it had been the work of angels, as Menander and Marcus hold, even if it had been the construction of some fiery being, likewise an angel, as Apelles teaches, the patronage of a secondary divinity would be enough for the dignity of the flesh. We know angels [as coming] next after God. Now then, whoever the supreme god of each heretic is, I would not without reason derive the dignity of the flesh from him too, since the will to produce it would have been present with him; for surely he would have prevented [it] from being made, which he knew was being made, if he had not wanted it to be made.
passages.notes: 'temperatur' is read as 'directed/aimed' (perhaps for 'temptatur'). 'frioulu' is a scanning error for 'friuolum'; 'uitupera.tione' for 'uituperatione'. 'Appelles' = Apelles.
